blogs.title: Procedure Without Payoff: The D.C. Circuit’s Standing Limit on Efforts to Compel OSC FOIA Investigations
blogs.description: This post would examine the court’s core holding that an asserted statutory right to an OSC investigation under 5 U.S.C. § 1216 cannot by itself support Article III standing. It would focus on the panel’s reliance on Summers, Lujan, and D.C. Circuit procedural-injury doctrine to reject a 'procedural right in vacuo,' and explain why the court found both of AFL’s asserted concrete interests inadequate. The post would highlight the opinion as a reminder that even mandatory-sounding statutory language ('shall conduct an investigation') does not eliminate the need for a plaintiff to show a concrete injury traceable to the defendant and likely redressable by judicial relief.

blogs.title: The Long Causal Chain Problem: How America First Legal Fits the Post-Hippocratic Medicine Standing Trend
blogs.description: This post would situate the decision within the Supreme Court’s recent tightening of causation and redressability analysis, especially where relief depends on the choices of third parties and enforcement officials. It would analyze the court’s emphasis on multiple discretionary actors—OSC, the MSPB, and DOJ—and its reliance on Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, Brackeen, Hecate Energy, and Heckler v. Chaney. The post would argue that the case reflects a broader doctrinal trend: plaintiffs increasingly cannot manufacture standing by asking courts to supervise one agency in hopes that another agency, or an adjudicatory body, will eventually change its behavior.

blogs.title: Section 1216, Section 552(a)(4)(F), and the Vanishing Merits: What the Standing Dismissal Leaves Unresolved About OSC’s FOIA Authority
blogs.description: This post would focus on the important statutory question the panel did not resolve: whether OSC’s investigative authority under § 1216 operates independently of FOIA’s more specific disciplinary trigger in § 552(a)(4)(F)(i). The district court had read § 1216 broadly but concluded that follow-on enforcement choices were discretionary; the D.C. Circuit vacated without reaching either issue. The post would explore the consequences of that nondecision for future litigants, including uncertainty over whether FOIA requesters can ever force OSC to consider arbitrary-withholding allegations before a court has entered a FOIA production order and fee award.

blogs.title: Informational Injury After Akins: Why Not Every Statutory Information Ecosystem Creates Standing
blogs.description: This post would analyze the opinion’s treatment of informational standing and its refusal to extend Akins and Public Citizen to OSC investigative processes. The panel drew a line between statutes that entitle a plaintiff to receive specified information and statutes that merely require an agency to investigate, even if information may emerge incidentally from that investigation. The post would explore the implications of that distinction for administrative-law plaintiffs who attempt to repackage disappointed enforcement requests as informational injuries, and for courts trying to police the boundary between genuine disclosure rights and indirect interests in agency oversight.
